base.title: 1 · Reading a card
base.body: Each card represents a radionuclide: an unstable isotope. Learn to recognise element, mass number, half-life, decay mode and context without memorising everything.

base.title: 2 · Protons, neutrons and isotopes
base.body: Protons define the element. Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

base.title: 3 · How the nucleus transforms
base.body: Alpha, beta-minus, beta-plus, electron capture and gamma transitions change the nucleus in different ways. Beta processes also involve neutrinos or antineutrinos, which interact very weakly.

base.title: 4 · Half-life
base.body: Half-life is statistical: after one half-life, on average, half of the undecayed nuclei remain and the activity is halved.

base.title: 5 · Where radionuclides appear
base.body: Medicine, natural radioactivity, radon, dating, industry and research show that radioactivity is not a single scenario with a single meaning.

base.title: 6 · Irradiation and contamination
base.body: Being exposed to radiation does not automatically make a person or object radioactive. Contamination means radioactive material is present on or inside something.

intermediate.title: 1 · From card to question
intermediate.body: A card combines several properties of one radionuclide. Explorer helps you connect each question to a scientific property, then uses automatic elimination so you can compare your reasoning.

intermediate.title: 2 · Element, isotope and nucleus
intermediate.body: Z is the proton number and identifies the element. A is the mass number. Isotopes of one element share Z but differ in neutron number N = A − Z.

intermediate.title: 3 · Decays and neutrinos
intermediate.body: In β− decay a neutron becomes a proton while an electron and an electron antineutrino are emitted. In β+ decay a proton becomes a neutron while a positron and an electron neutrino are emitted; electron capture also emits a neutrino. A γ transition de-excites the nucleus without changing A or Z.

intermediate.title: 4 · Decay mode is not the same as observed radiation
intermediate.body: Decay mode describes the nuclear transformation; particles or photons observed may be products of that transformation or of later processes. In PET, the radionuclide emits a positron and a neutrino, while the two 511 keV photons come from positron annihilation.

intermediate.title: 5 · Half-life and time scales
intermediate.body: Comparing orders of magnitude is often more useful than memorising exact values. Minutes, hours, days, years or billions of years can separate very different radionuclide groups.

intermediate.title: 6 · Medicine, nature, environment and research
intermediate.body: PET and SPECT rely on different emission properties; radionuclide therapy uses radiation to deposit dose in a target. Other radionuclides are natural, cosmogenic, or used in dating, industry and research.

expert.title: 1 · Scientist: explicit reasoning
expert.body: Scientist reduces scaffolding and uses manual elimination. Core properties include Z, A, N, nuclear transformations, quantitative half-life, applications and relationships among card properties.

expert.title: 2 · Z, A and N as constraints
expert.body: Z identifies the element, A counts nucleons and N = A − Z. Alpha decay changes A and Z; beta decays and electron capture keep A constant while Z changes by one unit.

expert.title: 3 · Conservation in beta decay
expert.body: β−: n → p + e− + ν̄e. β+: p → n + e+ + νe. Electron capture: p + e− → n + νe. The neutrino or antineutrino is essential for conservation of energy, momentum and lepton number, even though it is not a direct gameplay clue.

expert.title: 4 · Exponential decay law
expert.body: For an ensemble of nuclei N(t)=N0e^(−λt). T½ = ln2/λ and τ = 1/λ describe the same decay probability. An individual decay remains random.

expert.title: 5 · Decay mode and observed radiation
expert.body: Do not confuse the nuclear transformation with what a detector observes. A decay may leave a daughter nucleus excited; an emitted positron may later annihilate; γ photons can therefore appear as later products.

expert.title: 6 · PET, SPECT and therapy: the physics
expert.body: PET uses β+ emitters and detects annihilation photons in coincidence, not the neutrino. SPECT detects γ photons. In radionuclide therapy, radiation type influences dose deposition and the spatial scale of energy release.

base.title: 1 · How to read a card
base.body: Each card describes one radionuclide. Element, mass number, half-life, nuclear transformations and context are different properties; good questions use them to narrow the deck.

base.title: 2 · Element and isotope
base.body: The element is defined by proton number Z. Isotopes of the same element share Z but have different neutron numbers.

base.title: 3 · Half-life
base.body: Half-life is the time over which the average number of undecayed nuclei and the activity are reduced by one half. It does not predict when one nucleus will decay.

intermediate.title: 7 · Irradiation, contamination and risk
intermediate.body: Irradiation is exposure to radiation; contamination is the presence of radioactive material. Risk depends on amount, radiation type and energy, route of exposure, time, distance and context; the word “radioactive” alone does not determine risk.

expert.title: 7 · Risk and activation
expert.body: Exposure and contamination remain distinct. Ordinary irradiation does not automatically make matter radioactive; activation is a separate nuclear process requiring suitable projectiles or photons, energies and targets.

expert.title: 8 · Chemistry as a supporting property
expert.body: Every radionuclide belongs to an element with its own chemical family and physical state. These properties can support deduction, but they are not nuclear properties and must not be confused with decay mode.
